homes.heading: ### How this teacher explains
paragraphs: **This is how this teacher usually explains anything, on a Teach board in any kind of lesson or wherever else something is explained: the takeaway, then a because or so that explains that one key point, then an example or what it does not mean.** It is how he usually explains, not a template. The takeaway is on every Teach board, and the because or so is nearly always there with it: the reason is what turns a fact into something a child understands, and a board with the fact and no reason is a summary. The backstory that places the idea (who, where, what was happening, what life was like) is on the board too, because an idea with no story around it arrives from nowhere and a child cannot hold what they cannot place. The other parts, and anything else that teaches (a striking fact, a light line), go on when this moment needs them and in whatever order teaches it best, so the boards across a lesson vary rather than repeat one shape: his words, "I don't always want to see 5 things on every teach slide. I don't always want to see things in the same order every time." What decides it is a balance, and each part of it has its own way of going wrong:

- **Less is more, but less means fewer things, not shorter ones, and it has a floor.** A board with the few things that carry the idea is easier to take in than one holding everything true about it. Few is not fewest: three or four things is often right, and five, counting the picture, is the most (`preferences.md` → Pride Lessons, `How much a Teach slide holds`). The floor: if a teacher did nothing but read the board aloud, would the children still get what they need to do the next task and succeed? Each line is still a whole sentence a child can follow; a board cut down to a label and a slogan has thrown away the understanding it was there for. What goes when a board is too full is a repeat or an extra fact, never the backstory or the reason. The teacher, 27 September 2026, after `less is more` had been read as `the takeaway and little else` and a deck arrived with no scene, no backstory and one sentence per card: "I just wanted a little bit less, that's all." - **Assume the children know nothing about the topic, not that they can't think.** Plain words, the reason said out loud, an example they can picture. Never baby talk, and never the same idea explained three ways. Speak to them as a class that can think hard about something they have simply never met, and speak to them on the board too: `Imagine...`, `Look at her.`, `you`, `we`. The teacher on a deck of bare statements: "It's no longer talking to the children anymore." - **The slides carry the teaching; the teacher brings the rest.** A tired, brand-new or cover teacher who does not know the topic must be able to teach the idea from the board. But the board is the spine, not a script: it leaves room for the teacher's own questions, stories, examples and humour.

A light line sits outside this balance. It is never there to help a child succeed at the task, so the read-aloud floor and `fewer things` are not its test: it earns its place when the material hands it over, it is said the way the teacher would say it, and it does not crowd the teaching or land on a child (`teacher-voice.md` §4).

The field that carries it is `explanation` on this route's Teach and on a skill lesson's `teach`, `activity` on a skill `prepare` in `explanation` mode, `explanation` on a task lesson's `teach-needed`, `accurateExplanation` on a discovery `teach-why`, and `input` on a dialogic `grounding-input` when it explains. Two exceptions keep their own shape: a skills lesson's teaching board stays brief (`teaching-sequence-skill-based.md` → Cycles, and the beats around them), and a discovery lesson lands its takeaway at the end, because children reach it themselves (`teaching-sequence-discovery.md` → Teach why).

`explanation` is the teaching, as the child reads it: the route from the takeaway to the point where the class can use it. The fact is the destination; teaching is the route; the board carries the route (`preferences.md` → Slide Philosophy, `The fact is the destination`). (1) The takeaway, one sentence, which is the `headline` and usually the first thing on the board (`Lord Shaftesbury wanted children to spend less time working in factories.`). (2) The because or the so: the reason it is true or the thing it changes, said as a reason and not as another fact (`Long days at work left children tired, with little time to learn or play.`). This builds on the children’s working lives already established or briefly recalled. `Factory` may already be clear enough in context; the board need not define every concrete noun. Decide whether clarification is needed using the Vocabulary familiarity judgement, and supply useful support in the notes rather than assuming topic expertise. What it must avoid is asking children to unpack several unfamiliar ideas before the takeaway makes sense. A fact beside a fact is not this step: `He was a member of Parliament, known then as Lord Ashley.` names him and gives no reason. (3) The example, which is the thing the class looks at while you say it. **Write it on the board unless the board already makes it obvious which thing you mean**, because an example a child cannot find teaches nothing, and a line restating a picture that has already said it spends the board on words the class can see. It is obvious, and the step stays spoken, when the thing is the only thing on the board, or when the picture's own label names it: a diagram labelled `oesophagus` has written the example already, and the key question does the pointing (`Which part connects the mouth to the stomach?`). It is not obvious, and the example is a line, when the picture holds several things and yours is one of them (a mine scene with a child, a cart and a tunnel), when what they should notice is not in the picture at all (a portrait on the board while the example is what the laws actually said), or when the beat has no picture to point at, which is most of maths and any beat built on a rule. **What you write is what they will notice, not only the instruction to go and look.** `Look at her. She isn't being paid to do this.` is the teacher's own calibration and works, because the noticing follows the look. `Follow the tube down from the mouth on the diagram.` stops at the sending, so a teacher reading their own board aloud sounds like someone giving directions and the class arrives at nothing. Three science boards were written that way on 22 September 2026, on a diagram that already carried the labels they sent children to find. (4) What it does not mean, when the sentence invites a wrong reading (the paragraph below). What the class already has may open the route when the takeaway needs it (`Every home needs food, a fire and a roof, every single day.` before the Tudor sentence); it is the way in, not a fifth part. The parts are one sentence each, most of the time, and a beat that honestly has no reason to give or nothing to refuse leaves that part out rather than filling it. Saying the same thing three ways is a fault (this section's last paragraph: the landed sentence again in other words); walking the route is three or four different things and is the teaching itself. The script says the same essential route as spoken words, with connective talk and brief incidental explanations the board does not need. The board carries the knowledge and relationships the planned pupil task depends on; it does not transcribe every teacher explanation. The tell that the route stayed in the script is an essential reason or relationship the next task uses with no visible counterpart; the presence of `because`, `so` or a correction in notes alone is not sufficient evidence. Script lines such as `He wasn't a king who could order everybody to obey him`, `It wasn't the ten-hour law`, `People sometimes call the whole front of their body their tummy, but the stomach is this one organ` and `'Small' is doing a rather misleading job in that name`, are that tell when the planned task depends on them and they are said but never shown.

**The fourth part: when the sentence invites a wrong reading, refuse it on the same board.** Teaching creates misconceptions as it goes, and the truer the sentence the cleaner the wrong version of it. `Victorian children from poor families worked because their families needed the money` invites `so every Victorian child worked`, and a class carrying that away has learnt something false from something true. One line refuses it where it was created, in the same words the class has just heard: `That doesn't mean every Victorian child worked. Richer children usually went to school.` The wrong reading turns up in every subject. The sentence that refuses it is not one sentence you reuse. **Write the refusal as you would say it to this class, and let the wrong idea decide its shape.** The plain refusal above is one move. Often the truth said straight against the wrong version does it in one breath and needs no refusing at all (`The stomach is this one bag, up here, not your whole tummy.`). When the misleading thing is a word, take the word head on (`Small doesn't mean shorter. It describes how wide the tube is, and the small intestine is the longer one.`). When the class can settle it themselves, the honest move is not a statement: the wrong reading meets them in the Do that follows and the board carries the question. A deck whose every correction opens `That doesn't mean` has found one sentence and reused it, which is saying the same thing three ways, at the level of slides; the teacher's ruling: "we want variety, and sometimes it's not relevant just stating the misconception". `teacher-voice.md` §11 owns how a correction sounds. It is the boundary on this slide's own sentence, so it needs no entry in `misconceptions`, which holds the beliefs children arrive with.

The limit is the wrong idea a later beat has children correct themselves. This lesson's `fix the claim` beat on `their parents did not care about them` is worth far more as a sentence a child rewrites than as a line they read, and taking it away on the Teach slide spends the beat before they reach it. So ask which of the two a wrong idea is: one nothing downstream touches, which belongs here, or one a Do beat is built to expose, which does not. At most one boundary line per Teach slide; a second is usually a wrong idea nobody was having yet.

**Check the child’s route before the board’s shape.** Make sure children can enter the situation the takeaway answers: what is happening, who is affected and why this matters to them. When that background is already established, start with the takeaway and connect back to it in the reason; do not force another scene-setting slide. Use a familiar experience, an intelligible picture or a specific retrieval prompt where it helps; supply the reminder needed to enter the new teaching. Follow the same people and problem across beats, briefly reconnecting them after a change of focus. A story is a connected explanation, not invented dialogue or a compulsory fictional character. The usual takeaway → reason → example shape starts once children can understand its first sentence; a short lead-in can be on the same board or an earlier scene-setting board. Check what a child could now point to, describe or decide. Matching the four parts while filling them with unfamiliar abstractions has not taught the idea. Do not impose a story on a familiar procedure or add background that the current learning does not need.

**The first line a child reads uses only words they already have.** The landed sentence usually leads the board (a content Teach's `headline`, and its equivalent on every other route). Because it is read first, it can only use what the class has met by then, and so can the beat's `label`, which prints as the slide title above it (`What did Victorians think spread cholera?` named the disease two slides before the lesson brought it in). A hard word the board below is about to bring in is read before it is introduced, so the headline says it in words they already have and the new word arrives where the board sets its scene: on a Year 4 board about how Victorian families lived, `Victorians thought bad air caused cholera` sat above the lines that bring cholera in, where `Victorians thought bad air caused diseases` needs nothing the class does not have (the teacher, 28 September 2026: "just because there is a key vocab, doesn't mean it's introduced properly"). A vocabulary card shown earlier is not that introduction (`preferences.md` → `A name, or a thing the class has never met, arrives with its context in the sentence that brings it in`). The same holds for any topic word on a board: when a child would need to know it to follow the slide, it is explained in the sentence that brings it in or carded straight before that slide (`preferences.md` → Vocabulary).

**The test is a teacher who does not already know this content and has not opened the notes.** Could they teach from this board, on their first day? A picture with a label and one fact lets a teacher reading the board aloud say where the thing is and nothing else, so the children learn a label rather than what it names. A Year 4 history slide carried a photograph, `A Tudor farm household`, `England, 1485 to 1603` and one fact, with the route in the notes, and the user met it cold: "the scene hasn't been set; there's nothing on the slide to guide me to know what to say." The boards he chose instead are written out in `preferences.md` → Pride Lessons, `What a Teach slide holds`; write to them.

So the default is to write it, and the validator refuses `null` on a `teach` beat (a task lesson's `teach-needed` keeps its own rule: `null` only when the idea and its instance already carry the meaning). The PSHE slide that put `You can pass without giving a reason` on the board and left what pass means in the script is the same failure from the other end. The sentences are whole, warm sentences in the teacher's own register (`teacher-voice.md` §2): `In Tudor times there were no shops, and no light switches on the walls`, never `No shops, no switches`, because a clipped line is a label and the board is the same voice as the script with fewer sentences. Write the route in the order the class meets it, because when it will not fit one board at the ceiling (`Pride Lessons` → `How much a Teach slide holds`) the Slide Designer splits the beat where the teaching turns, the scene set on one slide and the look and the landed sentence on the next, with the picture on both; the words are never shrunk or clipped to fit. What the field is not is the landed sentence again in other words. The validator refuses the near-copy it can measure (the headline and the star line); a card that restates the headline with one detail added is yours to refuse. For the right to pass: `Sometimes you don't want to answer a question or share something personal. In PSHE, you can choose to pass.` / `You can say "I'd like to pass." You don't have to explain why.`

homes.heading: ### The launch
paragraphs: `launch` is `null` when children can begin from the question alone, or when an earlier beat of this lesson has already shown the class a good one of this product, and `goodLooksLike` is `null` when the success criteria already show what a good one looks like (an actual good one, such as a model answer or a good paragraph, never a list of what a good one includes).

**The instance is whatever the product actually is.** `words` carries it when children write; `show` names one of this beat's own `photoRefs` or `representationRefs` when they draw, build, sort or label, and both together are a written instance beside the thing it describes. Only `show` makes a launch for a labelled diagram show two diagrams rather than a sentence about what a good label says.

**`established` sets the case, not a recap.** When the task is about a particular case, this line is who it is, what happened and what they are being asked - the question the class holds while they look at the model, on its own short slide before it. A recap of what the lesson established is right only when there is no case to set, and it is `null` when the strong instance already carries it.

**`steps` are stages of work, not the standard said again.** Ask of each step whether the class would lose anything it cannot already see if it were deleted. A launch that shows a model, with the criteria visible while children work, has usually said all four of `read the case`, `use the criteria`, `write it as sentences` and `check each one leads to the next` already - on the case slide, in the criteria panel, in the two cards and in the `difference` line. Leave `steps` empty there; stages earn the field when they really happen in an order and the later ones are invisible until the earlier ones are done (make one, combine your group's, agree ours).

**`difference` is one line a child can check their own work against.** The two cards already show the contrast, so this line names what the strong one *does* that the weak one only states, in the words the success criteria or the steps already use. `Each sentence says what caused the next one.` passes; `Every sentence picks up the thing before it.` does not, because a child cannot test their own writing against it.

**The strong instance would meet this lesson's own success criteria.** Every `{{taught word}}` the beat's criteria name appears in it, and the validator refuses a model that leaves one out: a class shown a model that would fail the standard is being marked against something it was never shown.

**When the task asks children to explain, justify or say why, open `explanation-tasks.md`.** It owns `reasoningWords` (the few connecting words this task needs, by year group, faded as the class gets surer), `rehearsal` (say it to a partner, be asked one question, then write the second version), and the missing-link question that replaces "add more detail". A lesson can teach every subject word it names and still get four true sentences in a row, because the words that supply knowledge are not the words that connect it.

section.heading: ## Reference Files - precedence and decision-point loading

present.text: **Skill-based:** My Turn → Our Turn → Your Turn. Short explanation when skill needs it, else straight to model.
**Content-based:** Teach one manageable chunk → children use/process → next distinct chunk → larger practice drawing learning together, placed where the class is ready for it.
Both skill/content: children use/process one idea before different new idea. Explanation + model of same idea may be one block.

**Discovery:** Genuine route when observing/investigating phenomenon is best way to teach objective. All three must hold: enough prerequisite, phenomenon safe/dependable/revealing, explicit explanation follows securing why. Make judgement first; if doubtful after prerequisites/phenomenon/objective, teach directly.

For procedure, pattern investigation or method comparison may precede direct teaching when adds value, but novices must receive clear direct teaching and not invent complete procedure via unguided trial.
Smaller bounded exploration may sit inside skill/content.

The structure choice itself is made in the main agent's Structure Decision section. By the time this file is read, the structure decision and the boundary tests have already been applied — what follows is execution detail for the chosen rhythm.

When Dialogic is a candidate, read `lesson-designer-components.md` → Dialogic route before committing the structure. Its open-question, grounding, safety and synthesis boundaries still apply; a subject label does not choose the route.

When Task-Centred is a candidate, read `lesson-designer-components.md` → Task-Centred route before committing the structure, including when distinguishing one sustained task from repeated skill practice. Keep the writing-form boundary below in view.
**Writing lesson turns on whether form already child's.** "Produce extended writing" is task-centred only when child already commands form and today is carrying out piece.
So Skill-based with extended piece as optional Apply when earned. Give-away: learning to write this form or applying form already held?

**Splitting axis when LO names multiple outputs** (words+digital, add+subtract, pounds↔pence, standard+expanded, fraction+decimal): do outputs share one procedure or different? Same procedure different outputs = one concept (a/an: check next sound). Different procedures = two concepts
When LO has output fork AND directional/categorical fork (words vs digital × past vs to), split on output fork - not directional.
**Dialogic:** Objective requires forming/justifying position on genuinely contested/interpretive question, not recalling fact or performing skill. Subject label does not determine route.

Three conditions: genuinely contested/interpretive (multiple defensible positions), children have stake/anchor (lived experience, accessible scenarios, or prior content with substance), teacher scaffolds positions and surfaces multiple perspectives, not fixed answer.
Dialogic test: *defended position* vs *accurate account*. "what an influencer is" = Content-based; "should you trust an influencer's career advice?" = Dialogic. Same topic shifts by end task.

Dialogic may begin with small factual/vocab when needed. Teach necessary factual/legal/anatomical/statutory/safeguarding directly before judgement depending on it. If substantial new knowledge must be taught, use Content-based. Choose Dialogic because question permits several defensible positions and success is justified view, not because subject is PSHE/RE/History. Correct factual errors, safeguarding, harmful claims clearly; use discussion to pressure-test incomplete/contestable views.

After the final discussion, include one honest Synthesise beat. It names and compares the positions, frames or tensions that genuinely appeared. It must not invent class views or announce one predetermined answer. A separate individual Reflect is conditional and belongs in the ending.
The beats themselves (Stimulus → Talk pairs, the Synthesise, the Reflect) are owned by `teaching-sequence-dialogic.md`; follow it once the route is chosen.

**Task-Centred:** Built around one substantial task - plan/run enquiry, design/make product, fieldwork, extended writing in form child already writes, open maths investigation. Children apply knowledge/skills largely already held, enabling input only if genuinely needed, substantial doing time protected, finished in form completing task's purpose.
Weight: skill-based builds skill via repeated performance; content-based builds knowledge in chunks; both weight on acquiring. Task-centred weight on applying - one sustained task.
Outcome may be open or tightly funnelled (Y4 fair test where variable almost picks itself still task-centred). Openness is dial, not test.

section.heading: ## 9. Lesson Structures — When Each Is Evidence-Based

present.text: **Use when.** Children are learning a repeatable skill or procedure they need to perform reliably.
**Structure.** A short explanation when the skill needs it → My Turn → enough guided practice for the likely difficulty → Your Turn → optional Apply.

One teaching cycle may contain closely connected, manageable variations of the same procedure; separate cycles are needed when combining them makes the procedure too complex or changes the decision rule.

**Why.** Modelling and supported practice expose the process and reduce unproductive search. A bounded pattern investigation or method comparison may precede direct teaching when it adds learning value, but novices are not left to invent the complete procedure unaided.
**Use when.** Children are learning a coherent body of knowledge, explanation or conceptual relationship they need to understand, recall or explain.

**Structure.** Teach one small, manageable chunk → children use or process it → teach the next distinct chunk → larger practice that draws the lesson's knowledge together, placed where the class is ready for it.
Main practice is not restricted to a question count or one written form, and Apply is optional.
**Why.** Small chunks protect working memory, while immediate processing makes children work with each idea before a different one arrives.

**Use when.** Discovery is the best route after judging the objective, children's prerequisite knowledge and a safe, dependable phenomenon. Explicit explanation afterwards secures why the result or pattern occurred.

**Why the caveats matter.** The evidence cautions against minimal guidance, not against Discovery as a full route. Productive Discovery is bounded, focused and followed by accurate explanation. It may also appear as a smaller exploration inside Skill-based or Content-based teaching.

**Procedure boundary.** A pattern investigation or method comparison may precede direct teaching of a procedure when it genuinely helps. Novices must not be left to invent the complete method through unguided trial and error.
**Safeguard.** Make the suitability judgement first. If productive Discovery still looks doubtful after considering the prerequisites, phenomenon and objective, teach the learning directly.
**Sequence.** Follow `teaching-sequence-discovery.md`.

**Use when.** The LO's success criterion is *the child can articulate and justify a position*, not recall a fact or perform a skill. Three conditions must hold: (a) the question is genuinely contested or interpretive — multiple defensible positions exist; (b) children have a stake or anchor to speak from — lived experience, accessible scenarios, or prior content knowledge with substance; (c) the teacher scaffolds positions and surfaces multiple views rather than delivering a fixed answer.

present.text: My Turn → Our Turn → Your Turn is the core rhythm. Add a short explanation before My Turn when the actual skill needs one; otherwise move straight into modelling.
A short pattern investigation or method comparison may come before direct modelling when it genuinely helps children notice the structure.

So may a **bounded first attempt** at the target itself — a few minutes with the real equipment or task before any model: *Can you make the bulb light?* Use it only when the attempt is safe, cheap and quick to reset, the goal is self-evident, and success or failure is visible to the child without the teacher judging it.
The attempt teaches nothing by itself and is not discovery; its job is to give the full modelling that follows immediately something real to explain

Do not use it where a wrong attempt looks fine to the child or quietly rehearses an error — a circuit fails visibly, a written calculation method fails silently — and `subject-maths.md` owns the maths opening decision.
Either way it remains part of the Skill-based route: the procedure is then explicitly explained, modelled and secured rather than left for novices to invent through unguided trial and error.

**A bounded attempt only works while the answer is still the child's to find.** Audit everything the class meets before it - the starter, the vocabulary cards, every visible reference and photograph - and keep the successful arrangement, rule or answer the attempt exists to expose out of all of it.
This audit is part of choosing the attempt, and the reviewer checks it: an attempt whose answer is already on display is a purposeful design defect, not polish.

For each skill being taught, design a My Turn → Our Turn → Your Turn sequence. Small variations of one procedure may share a cycle only when they are closely connected and easy enough to learn together. Split them when combining the variations creates too much complexity, even if they belong to the same broad procedure.
**My Turn** — the teacher demonstrates the whole method or skill with a specific example.

Choose the example carefully: it should make the concept clear without unnecessary complexity. The first example is a minimum-viable case — clean, unambiguous, easy to follow. If a second example is needed (to show a boundary case or common variation), it comes after the first, not instead of it.
**Choose modelled and guided examples by preparation and readiness.** A lengthy example may need one clear demonstration; quick instances may benefit from several carefully varied examples.

Select enough guided work to prepare the independent cases without repeating an already secure move merely to fill a pattern. Case coverage and the difficulty of the move govern the choice within the lesson time.
**Model every distinct case the independent practice will require.**

When the Your Turn will mix those cases, the child needs to have *seen each one worked* before meeting it alone, because a case modelled nowhere but appearing in independent practice is a case the child meets cold.
The failure to avoid is spending both My Turn examples on the same case while another case goes unmodelled: it looks like two worked examples, but it leaves a hole the Your Turn drops into.
**Coverage decides which examples appear; choose *which ones* so that what changes between them is what you want children to notice.**

So pick the first example as the cleanest instance of the method, with nothing incidental in it to distract from the steps, and pick each one after it to move the single feature the children need to see next.

The limit: this governs consecutive examples inside one concept, and it does not override the distinct-case coverage above, which sometimes needs a bigger jump to reach an unmodelled case. Deliberately varying a surface feature is also right when the teaching point is that the feature is irrelevant, for example changing the units or the names to show the method does not care about them.

When the teacher's brief names a number of modelled examples that is fewer than the number of distinct cases — "my turn, 2 questions" for a skill with three positions — coverage governs. Model each distinct case as its own worked example, and record the adjustment and its reason in design-decisions.md so the final hand-off stays anchored to the coverage decision.
**When the new learning is a *tool* applied to familiar content, keep the modelling's cases clear and let the Your Turn carry the real discrimination.**
Concretely for a sorting tool: if My Turn and Our Turn sorted shapes by one criteria pair, give the Your Turn a *different* criteria pair, so the same familiar shapes land in new regions
**Some skills are recognition, not procedure — and they are taught by establishing the set, not by modelling a method.**
**A process must be modelled, not displayed as its own output.**
The success criteria belongs on this slide as a live reference, visible while the teacher models

Any visual tool children will use (a number line, a classification table, a diagram) should be on the My Turn slide. Children need to see the tool in use during modelling so they know how to use it themselves.
**Some skills transform a whole text from one form into another, and the material the child works from must be the start form, complete and unconverted.**
**Build towards the integrated transformation.**

**Describe the modelled experience through the resource state.** Follow `references/modelling-formats.md` and state what later resources must provide: a prepared completed example, a blank or partly blank helper for live completion, the exact question and useful references while working is modelled elsewhere, or suitable support for a physical demonstration. Children must still see the important process, choices and checks a novice would otherwise miss. A prepared finished example is valid when inspecting the finished form is the useful teaching experience, but it cannot replace seeing a process carried out when producing the answer is the learning.

Plan enough Our Turn work for the concept's likely difficulty. If the concept looks tricky, include several fresh guided attempts rather than defaulting to one. The live teacher may skip planned guided examples when the real class is ready.
**When a concept records what children have just done, one model then release is the default.**
Add an Our Turn there only when the representation itself carries a hard new convention (formal notation, a symbol system) that one model will predictably fail to secure.

**Your Turn** — enough meaningful independent practice for the target action, cases and response cost. A compact table or sort may contain many brief decisions, while one whole passage, investigation step or constructed representation may be one substantial performance.
Follow definite-answer work with an answer slide.
Plan guided practice so successful independence is plausible. The live teacher decides from the real class whether to release, skip a planned guided example or add further support.
**Independent work means that children do the important thinking themselves.** Keep, reduce or remove each support according to the target thinking rather than the stage label.
- Remove or reduce a support when consulting it would perform the new thinking children are meant to do independently.

- A worked example may remain when it is genuinely the most useful quality reference, comparison model or reference support and children must still generate the important answer or decision themselves.
- Do not require a full → partial → blank fade across a set or assume a support must disappear by Your Turn.

Read the independent task and ask what the child still has to decide, produce, explain or perform. That answer, not the presence or absence of a scaffold, determines whether the work is independent, and it is what the Your Turn's `thinking` line says.

**Execution before selection is a strong default for a genuinely new repeatable method.** Normally secure reasonable execution before asking children to choose when, why or how to use the method. Do not manufacture a separate fluency phase when judgement or selection is inseparable from the skill itself. In maths, fluency-first remains a strong available lesson shape when it fits; `subject-maths.md` owns that subject-specific judgement.

Independent practice in a skill-based lesson is focused and repeated, because the goal is reliable execution: until the procedure is automated it consumes the working memory the child needs for anything richer. Order the set by variation theory — keep most features constant, change one — so the child sees what matters and what doesn't.

Then decide whether the instances should stand separately or be organised so their relationship is visible. Keep related results together when noticing the invariant or contrast is part of the learning; separate them when each instance requires independent selection or working and its neighbours would become a cue.

The boundary is the integrated task: transforming one whole passage or constructing one complete representation may be enough because the target action itself is extended. Do not multiply it into fragments to satisfy a repetition count.
Once it has a competitor (the other rule, the confusable category, last week's method), mix the cases rather than running a long row of near-identical items

Two warnings ride with this rule. Mixed practice looks worse in the lesson — more errors, children feeling less sure — and wins later, so it is not judged by how the lesson felt. And the direct evidence outside maths is thin (a small number of studies), so this is the better bet, not the proven answer.

present.text: When the success criteria for a concept is a procedure written as how-to steps, these are the mechanics of writing those steps well.
**Writing how-to steps:** Each step is one verb-first action, written so that a child who is stuck, with the teaching over, can do it from the words alone.
**Steps go wrong in two directions, and the fix for one is not the fix for the other.**
*Too short to run.* The step names a stage and leaves the child to supply the method
*Too long to use.* The step carries teaching the child has already had
- The explanation.
- The alternatives.

- The explanation. `Multiply the whole pounds by 100 (this converts them to pence)` repeats the teaching inside the step; `Multiply the pounds by 100.` is the move. An accuracy reminder is not an explanation: `keeping any zeros it needs` may earn its own step when children need it. Do not hide necessary new teaching in notes or delete it to shorten the criteria. - The alternatives. `Connect the switch to the lamp or buzzer`, four times down a list, spends most of the panel on a choice the teacher makes once. Name one piece of equipment and let the teacher say the class is using buzzers. - A case the method already handles. Omit a separate reminder when the ordinary steps already give the right result. Frequency alone is not a reason to remove a necessary decision: keep a required branch as a sentence or short question (`If you have ten ones, exchange them for one ten.`), or use a lookup table when several cases are easier to scan there. The guide must be available at that point and stay within the stage's taught scope; explanations and extra knowledge remain in teaching or sticky knowledge.
**Say how, unless the class can already do it without thinking.**
**A step is written in the child's own words, not the plan's.**
**The steps are the procedure in the order the child performs it.**
**Steps encode the decision rule, never an artefact of the worked example.**
The same mechanics hold outside maths. A PE throwing lesson:
Good: "Point your other arm at the target."
**Name a familiar action only when children genuinely know how to carry it out from earlier lessons.**
**When several cases need a lookup** - for example a conversion where the direction changes the operation - name each row using the actual content the child sees, not an abstract category label.
Name the content, not the category. The same principle applies to any branch, in any subject.

When a task genuinely branches, use the clearest child-runnable guide: a table, flowchart, short decision list or another suitable form. Do not default to a flowchart or create a branching guide for a simple non-branching method.
- **Phrase each branch as the question the child asks**
- **Name the cases in one consistent scheme the child can map onto any instance.**
- **Keep the action half parallel so only the deciding part changes down the column.**
- **Keep each cell short — a glance reference, not a sentence.**
- **Order the rows in a sequence the child can anticipate.**
- **Pick out the one word that changes between rows.**
The aim throughout is a table the child can *run*
**One concept, one SC.** Each concept teaches one thing end-to-end and carries one success criteria.
**The SC must not change across My Turn, Our Turn, and Your Turn.**
**When Concept 2 wraps around Concept 1's procedure, carry the steps it needs into Concept 2's SC in Concept 1's own words.**

present.text: - Keep the starter focused. Mixed recent and older retrieval is a sequence-level option when the teacher requests it or the wider sequence gives it a clear purpose and relevant methods or knowledge are secure enough to discriminate.
- Use the simplest form that retrieves the intended learning accurately. A short question set, matching, sorting, correction, labelling or one rich problem may each be right.

**Avoid.** Long "warm-ups" that become mini-lessons. Silent copying. Questions so hard that they re-teach rather than strengthen. Mixing older material without a sequence purpose or before pupils have enough security to choose productively.
**Principle.** Novices learn procedures and concepts fastest from fully worked examples and explicit modelling, not from solving problems unaided. Rosenshine #4 (models).
A model that voices the thinking ("I notice… I need to… I'll check…") directs their thought at the *reasoning*, not just the surface form.
The menu, each with the condition it suits:

- **Critique a flawed / erroneous example** ("spot the mistake", a non-example) — when the lesson turns on a strong, predictable misconception (confront it head-on rather than hope it never forms — see §5); when you want pupils *processing* the rule rather than watching it; and when they *own* the outcome (their own plan, their own piece), where a full model hands them a template to copy but a broken one shows the rules in play without giving the answer.
- **A single neutral warm-up** — when the move can be shown on a throwaway case without giving away the real task; one only, never a string of decoys.

These are not exclusive — model *then* critique, or critique *then* practise, are common. The discipline is to choose for *this* lesson by asking: do they have the prior schema? does the lesson turn on a known misconception? do the children own the outcome? who will stall, and what gives them an anchor? is the skill best shown live? — rather than letting the structure's usual move pick itself.

**The move and the instance.** When you model a transferable move live — finding a fact and shortening it to a note, composing a sentence, taking a reading — distinguish the *move* being taught from the specific *instance* used to demonstrate it, but normally supply both.
The active part of a live-complete helper stays constructable, but the teacher is not left to invent the instance itself.

- When live modelling is chosen, expose the process, decisions and checks children need to see. Use a prepared completed example when inspecting the finished form is the useful teaching experience; do not substitute it when children need to see the process produced.

- Choose the number of worked or modelled examples from the learning, the time each takes, the genuinely distinct cases and the lesson time. Begin with the simplest representative example and add another only when it teaches a useful variation, case or boundary.
- Pair spoken explanation with a useful visual or representation when that combination supports the learning.
- Keep, reduce or remove support according to whether it enables the intended thinking or supplies that thinking or answer.
**Avoid.** The **expertise reversal effect** (Kalyuga): heavy scaffolding that helps novices *hurts* pupils who already have the schema.

What this does not rule out is a deliberately chosen problem-first opening whose purpose is to prepare children for the explanation rather than to make them discover it: a bounded observation before the Teach that secures its meaning (`teaching-sequence-content-based.md`), a flawed example to critique before children attempt their own, or a full Discovery route where the three conditions hold.

**In content lessons** (science, history, geography, RE), practice combines remembering and reasoning, with meaningful reasoning appearing early enough to form part of the core work every child is expected to reach.
Writing about content can help children organise, express and consolidate understanding, but it is one useful option rather than a compulsory ingredient in every lesson.
**In writing lessons**, the practice is composing, with support, using a taught and memorised process — the best-evidenced move in primary writing by a distance
so a lesson that teaches a component builds the bridge deliberately: the child uses it inside real composing in the same lesson or the next, because the transfer does not happen on its own.
**A repetition earns its place by changing something.**
**Avoid.** "Differentiation by outcome" where low attainers drift without a teacher. Pages of identical questions with no variation — this plateaus learning.

**Principle.** Plan for the genuine specific misconceptions a topic reliably produces — often one to three, sometimes one, and sometimes none worth a separate teaching beat. Surface important ones deliberately during teaching rather than relying on later marking.
- Identify the canonical misconceptions the topic genuinely has before designing the lesson — the count is the topic's own, not a target.
- Show a wrong answer on a slide — "this pupil got 0.7. What did they do? Why is it wrong?" — and discuss. This is safer than letting it happen silently in books.
- Address the misconception with a counter-example, not just a correction. "If that rule were true, then…" lets pupils see the contradiction.
- Revisit an important misconception in a later lesson only when the user supplies genuine sequence context, linked files or assessment evidence. Do not invent an unknown next lesson.
Fix it by holding everything else constant — same subject, same context — and varying only the taught feature, then phrasing the question on that feature.

For persuade-vs-describe, both notes should be about the *same* attraction — "The Colosseum is a large stone amphitheatre" (describes) vs "You'll stand where real gladiators once fought!" (sells) — and the question asks "which one *sells* the place?", not "which *belongs* in a brochure?", because a plain describing line can legitimately belong in one.

**Avoid.** Only teaching the correct method and hoping the misconception never forms. Correcting misconceptions privately one book at a time when they are in fact shared by half the class. Treating a misconception as carelessness — it is usually a mis-generalised rule.
- The teacher, not the generated resource, decides from the real response whether to proceed, re-explain or add guided practice.

Two different wrong ideas usually want two different moves - a shared misconception wants the point re-explained on a changed example or representation, a class split between two conceptions wants the two compared openly, right answers with weak reasons want the explanation asked for rather than the score accepted - and naming them is a teaching judgement the design can make in advance.
Prescribing cold call, no hands, wait time, Everybody Writes, Show Call, books, whiteboards or a fixed sampling routine.
**Principle.** Protect working memory ruthlessly. Every extraneous element on a slide, every redundant sentence, every split attention point steals capacity from learning.
Slide design is almost entirely about eliminating extraneous load.

- **Split-attention effect.** Put labels on the diagram, not in a separate key. Put the question and its working in the same visual field. Don't make pupils hold one thing in mind while looking at another.

- **Redundancy effect.** Do not put the teacher's script on the slide and also say it. Pupils try to read and listen simultaneously and do both badly. Slides carry the image/diagram/worked example; the teacher carries the narration.
- **Modality effect.** Visual + spoken beats visual + written for explanations. Use the slide for the diagram, your voice for the commentary.
- **Coherence.** Relevant optional context pictures are governed by `context-pictures.md` and must disappear rather than reduce text, work space, clarity or completion speed.

**Avoid.** Walls of text. Multiple representations of the same thing that pupils must integrate (split attention). Teacher reading the slide. Animations that move while you explain — the eye tracks the motion instead of the meaning.

**Principle.** Every lesson should end with purposeful consolidation or useful evidence, in the form that completes its structure. Same-session retrieval is one possible ending, not a universal exit-ticket requirement.
- Choose the ending that best completes the lesson's actual work.
- Do not prescribe the recording medium or a fixed question/time count.
- Use the ending to shape a linked next lesson only when the user supplies genuine sequence context or real assessment evidence.
- Without that context, do not invent class results, apply a fixed threshold or prescribe tomorrow's lesson.

Where the sequence context is supplied, that naming becomes a real link; where it is not, it is still the honest answer to "what would be lost if nobody asked for this again", and the teacher decides what to do with it.

**Avoid.** Adding an exit ticket that duplicates the ending already present; forcing every ending into silent written retrieval; relying on volunteers as the only evidence; inventing a next-day re-teach need from results the resource cannot know.

- **High success is conditional, not one universal metric.** For a defined repeatable skill, roughly 80% success at release is a useful planning expectation; it does not govern every lesson type, generated resources cannot know the real result, and success above 95% is not automatically unproductive.
- **Dual coding** in explanations; **variation theory** in practice questions.

present.text: **The fourth part: when the sentence invites a wrong reading, refuse it on the same board.** Teaching creates misconceptions as it goes, and the truer the sentence the cleaner the wrong version of it. `Victorian children from poor families worked because their families needed the money` invites `so every Victorian child worked`, and a class carrying that away has learnt something false from something true. One line refuses it where it was created, in the same words the class has just heard: `That doesn't mean every Victorian child worked. Richer children usually went to school.` The wrong reading turns up in every subject. The sentence that refuses it is not one sentence you reuse. **Write the refusal as you would say it to this class, and let the wrong idea decide its shape.** The plain refusal above is one move. Often the truth said straight against the wrong version does it in one breath and needs no refusing at all (`The stomach is this one bag, up here, not your whole tummy.`). When the misleading thing is a word, take the word head on (`Small doesn't mean shorter. It describes how wide the tube is, and the small intestine is the longer one.`). When the class can settle it themselves, the honest move is not a statement: the wrong reading meets them in the Do that follows and the board carries the question. A deck whose every correction opens `That doesn't mean` has found one sentence and reused it, which is saying the same thing three ways, at the level of slides; the teacher's ruling: "we want variety, and sometimes it's not relevant just stating the misconception". `teacher-voice.md` §11 owns how a correction sounds. It is the boundary on this slide's own sentence, so it needs no entry in `misconceptions`, which holds the beliefs children arrive with.
